lead: On the grid, the inverter does not set the voltage. The grid sets it, and the inverter injects a controlled sine current. A phase-locked loop (PLL) finds the grid angle θ; a slower power loop sets the current amplitude; a fast current loop switches the bridge so the measured current follows the reference. Rooftop solar, battery storage and wind converters use this scheme. It also sets power factor, limits harmonics, and detects an island. This chapter covers the loops, the controllers and the filter.
prereq: You need: Chapters 4.4 and 4.5 for the modulator; Unit 6 for PV and storage context.

sections.h3: The grid sets voltage, the inverter sets current

blocks.text: A utility grid is a stiff voltage source. Its voltage amplitude and frequency stay nearly fixed while loads change. If a grid-tied inverter also tried to set voltage, two voltage sources joined by a cable would fight; the current would be set only by the small difference between them. Instead the inverter works as a current source. It measures grid voltage, locks to its angle, and injects a current of the size and phase it wants. The grid absorbs that current.

The PLL gives θ, the grid angle in radians. A DC-link or maximum-power-point-tracking (MPPT) loop compares available DC power with delivered AC power and sets I*, the peak current reference in amperes. A nonzero φ* commands reactive power.

blocks.where: i* is the current reference in A; I* is its peak in A; θ is the grid angle in rad from the PLL; φ* is the commanded phase shift in rad (0 for unity power factor).

blocks.text: Single-phase real power is P = V_rms I_rms cos φ, where V_rms and I_rms are rms grid voltage and current in volts and amperes, and φ is the phase angle between them. In three-phase, P = √3 V_LL I_rms cos φ, with V_LL the line-to-line rms voltage in volts.

items: Measure grid voltage; the PLL gives θ and frequency.
The slower power loop sets I* from the DC-link error or MPPT.
Form i* from θ, I* and the commanded φ*.
The current controller compares measured i with i* and drives the bridge through PWM.
The LCL filter attenuates switching harmonics before the current enters the grid.

sections.h3: Three current controllers and the LCL filter

blocks.text: The current loop must be faster than the power loop. A power loop at 10–20 Hz is enough; a current loop often runs at 1–2 kHz.

Hysteresis control compares measured current i with a band of width h around i*. When i reaches i* + h/2, the bridge switches one way; at i* − h/2, it switches back. It is simple and robust, but switching frequency varies with current slope and grid voltage, so the filter is harder to design.

In the synchronous dq frame, the PLL angle rotates the measured currents into DC quantities i_d and i_q. PI controllers drive their errors to zero; the integrator gives zero steady-state error at the fundamental. The axes are coupled by ωL, where ω = 2πf is grid angular frequency in rad/s and L is the filter inductance in henry. Decoupling adds ±ωL i_q and ∓ωL i_d so one axis does not disturb the other. The bridge then switches at a fixed PWM frequency.

A proportional-resonant (PR) controller works in the stationary frame. G_PR(s) = K_p + K_r s/(s² + ω₀²), where s is the Laplace variable, K_p is proportional gain, K_r is resonant gain, and ω₀ = 2πf₀ is the fundamental angular frequency in rad/s. It gives large gain at f₀ and no transform is needed.

An LCL filter has inverter-side inductance L1, grid-side inductance L2 and shunt capacitance C. It attenuates switching harmonics faster than a single L. Its resonance f_res = (1/2π)√((L1+L2)/(L1L2C)) must be damped, by a resistor or active damping, or the loop can oscillate. Here f_res is in hertz, L1 and L2 in henry, C in farad.

sections.h3: Islanding, power factor and off-grid contrast

blocks.text: Anti-islanding protection stops the inverter when the grid disconnects. Otherwise it could energise a local line and endanger a lineman. Passive methods watch voltage and frequency; active methods inject a small disturbance and check the response. Standard tests require a trip within a set time.

Non-unity power factor is commanded by φ*. A phase shift makes the inverter deliver or absorb reactive power within the grid code. The current amplitude then follows the power demand and the reactive limit.

An off-grid inverter has no stiff grid. It must set voltage amplitude and frequency itself, so it uses a voltage loop, often with droop. It has no PLL to a live grid. A grid-tied unit sets current. Some inverters switch between both modes when the grid fails.

figure.caption: Power flows from the DC link through the bridge and LCL filter to the grid. Notice that the PLL feeds the grid angle to the current controller, which closes the loop back to the bridge.

spec.title: Grid-tied inverter control
spec.aria: Power flows from the DC link through the bridge and LCL filter to the grid, while a PLL reads the grid angle and a current controller drives the bridge.

examples.question: A rooftop solar inverter delivers P = 5 kW to a 230 V, 50 Hz single-phase grid at unity power factor. Find the rms and peak grid current reference. The grid voltage then rises to 240 V while the DC power stays 5 kW; find the new rms current. Explain why the amplitude must come from the power loop.
steps: At unity power factor cos φ = 1, so I_rms = P/V_rms = 5000 W ÷ 230 V = 21.739 A rms, which rounds to 21.7 A rms.
The peak reference is I* = √2 × I_rms = 1.4142 × 21.739 A = 30.744 A, which rounds to 30.7 A peak.
At V_rms = 240 V, I_rms = 5000 W ÷ 240 V = 20.833 A rms, which rounds to 20.8 A rms.
A fixed 21.739 A reference would give 240 V × 21.739 A = 5217 W at 240 V. The power loop must reduce I* to hold 5 kW.
The PLL keeps θ at the grid angle; with i* = I* sin θ, the current stays in phase with voltage at unity power factor.
examples.answer: The reference is 21.7 A rms (30.7 A peak) at 230 V and 20.8 A rms at 240 V; the power loop must set the amplitude.

traps: Commanding a voltage amplitude on a grid-tied inverter, or omitting the PLL, makes the current land at the wrong phase and the inverter push reactive power.
Mixing rms and peak current references: the sine table and comparator use the peak I*, while cable and meter ratings use rms.
Using the three-phase formula with phase voltage instead of line-to-line voltage, or forgetting √3, gives a current larger by √3.
Treating an LCL filter as a plain L and ignoring its resonance; without damping the current loop can oscillate near f_res.
Assuming anti-islanding means the inverter keeps running in an island; it must trip, while an off-grid inverter is designed to run without the grid.

quiz.q: What does the PLL supply to the current controller?
quiz.a: The grid angle θ and frequency, so the current reference has the correct phase.

quiz.q: Why is a grid-tied inverter controlled as a current source rather than a voltage source?
quiz.a: The grid already sets voltage; a second voltage source would only create current through the impedance difference, so the inverter commands current.

quiz.q: A 10 kW single-phase inverter feeds a 230 V, 50 Hz grid at unity power factor. Find the rms and peak current references.
Compare hysteresis and dq PI current control on switching frequency and steady-state error.
quiz.a: Hysteresis is simple with variable switching frequency and band-limited ripple; dq PI has fixed PWM frequency, needs decoupling, and its integrator gives zero steady-state error at the fundamental.

quiz.q: A three-phase 10 kW inverter connects to a 400 V line-to-line, 50 Hz grid at unity power factor. Find the line current.
Why does an LCL filter need damping, and what happens if it is not damped?
quiz.a: It has a resonance; undamped, switching or grid disturbances can excite it and the current loop can oscillate or become unstable.

quiz.q: State the purpose of anti-islanding in a grid-tied inverter.
quiz.a: To stop injection quickly when the grid is lost, protecting people and equipment from an energised island.

quiz.q: How does an off-grid inverter's control differ from a grid-tied one?
quiz.a: Off-grid sets voltage and frequency with its own oscillator and voltage loop; grid-tied follows grid angle and sets current.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production units add grid-code ride-through, weak-grid impedance estimation, and adaptive PLLs for low-inertia grids. Researchers study grid-forming control, where an inverter sets voltage and frequency like a synchronous machine. Search terms: grid-forming inverter, virtual synchronous generator, impedance-based stability, active damping.
